1.t: Banjo and guitar players and their beat
1.s: He names banjo and guitar players and describes their straight-four rhythm.
1.q: Banjo players and guitar players? Well it was John Marrera, Caffrey D'Aaron's Boyd, and Son Thomas, and Henry Kimmel. And Cells. They were terrific. And Caffrey D'Aaron's Boyd was one of them. John Marrera basically played, you know, the beat. Real great. John Marrera was a, I should say, name.…

1.t: Veined hands, Piku and Tony, and a photo of Snooks Eaglin
1.s: Remarks on a man's veins, a failed attempt to place Tony, and an introduction to a photo of Snooks Eaglin.
1.q: Quite a few guys in New Orleans have all them veins on your hands.

1.t: Danny Barker on his guitar playing and wish to be a writer
1.s: The host asks Barker about himself; he talks about playing rhythm guitar in New York bands and being a frustrated writer.
1.q: Because I think the people I think we ought to know something about you Your instrument Has your instrument always been the guitar Yes, I play guitar You know, play a little There's so much to learn about a guitar You know, and I start playing rhythm and bands and and getting in New York There's so…

1.t: Watching the town's banjo players and sitting in at the Alley Club
1.s: After the juke box thinned out work, Barker watched Johnny Davis, Son Thomas, the Marreros and others, and filled in for Caffrey Darensbourg at a downtown club.
1.ch: The banjo, rhythm and the New Orleans style
1.q: You’re around there. You see bands, so you’re going to decide whether you’re going to play music for a living or you’re going to cop out and do it pasttime. But it’s kind of rough playing, always was playing music for a living in New Orleans, because there’s so many musicians and so many clubs. And…

1.t: Chord symbols, rhythm guitar and the first electric guitar
1.s: Guitarists read chord symbols rather than notes, and Barker describes how arrangements left space for the guitar and the electric guitar's dangers.
1.q: Yeah, because a lot of arrangers didn’t know how to arrange for guitar, so there was very simple things. Even a commercial orchestration you bought, there was always a symbol. C 7 flat 5th, C 7 9th, C 7 this, B-flat 7 augmented 5th. This has that, and you know what a C 7 was. You had the 5th in it.…

1.t: Playing unamplified with the rhythm section
1.s: Barker explains how guitar and bass locked in without amplification, downstroke and upstroke technique, and Basie's chomping rhythm section.
1.q: You could feel it without the electricity. Or the bass coordinates. You and the bass hit that thump together, and you could hear it. The arrangers didn’t make the arrangement too compact to overshadow the openings.

1.t: Arrangers and rhythm guitarists: Trueheart, Holiday, Eddie Durham
1.s: He names arrangers and guitarists whose work he learned from, with John Trueheart of Chick Webb's band and Clarence Holiday as the standard-setters.
1.q: You stayed closest to the harmony that you could. You don’t want to be contrary. You run a series of C chords. C diminished. C augmented. Whatever it is. And you stay there. The bandleader trusts you to do the best you can, and you do the best you can from your knowledge what that sequence.

1.t: Benny Carter's band, Les Paul and the unnoticed rhythm man
1.s: After Benny Carter's praise Barker explains that critics ignore rhythm guitarists, citing Down Beat polls and Les Paul's Harlem shows.
1.q: Les Paul. I saw him on a thing the other night. That’s somebody who’s played so much guitar in them days. He . . . funny. He got famous and made that record. Can’t think of the name of the record. Electric. He had that work, that electric guitar. He’d work it up to almost a perfection of that time.…

1.t: Rhythm style on the Marsalis record and the six-string banjo
1.s: He describes the figure-eight rhythm on the Majesty of the Blues sessions, modelled on Johnny St. Cyr, and audiences' prejudice against banjos.
1.q: I didn’t do no single picking. I just put some rhythm that goes way back in New Orleans playing. That’s what them people . . . They put the rigamarolle, figure-eight strokes. It does something to people. It make people want to dance, because it’s rhythmic, and it’s not plink plank and plank plank…

1.t: Strolling blues guitarists and the legend of Stave-and-Chain
1.s: He recalls street guitarists like Black Hamp, Washburn guitars, and blues folk tales such as Stave-and-Chain.
1.ch: Wagon bands, halls and the old brass bands
1.q: But getting back to this music, there was music all around. Everywhere that guys could whistle. There was a strollin' guitar [gi-tar] player, a guy who played guitar who was known in the town -- Black Hamp and...Black Nolan(?). Helluva guitar player. That Folk guitar, that Leadbelly (?) that you…

1.t: Marvin Kimball, the showman banjoist with Papa Celestin
1.s: Kimball twirled his Paramount banjo and played it behind his head with Celestin's band.
1.ch: A musical family and the old New Orleans bands
1.q: And right away you begin to learn who carries weight, and who can play and who can't play and who is copying. Well, right away, when I looked around, I saw Kimball.

1.t: New York's guitar and banjo players: Bobby Johnson, Truehart, Clarence Holiday
1.s: On arriving in New York, Danny noticed virtuoso banjoists struggling while rhythm players like John Truehart and Clarence Holiday anchored big bands.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: I found when I got to New York... I looked around and saw all the virtuoso guitar players (there wasn't many [?] banjo players, and they weren't doing much. They were with tramp bands, or they were working in dives and... I saw Banjo Bernie come through, and I saw Speed, Speedy... Speedy worked…

1.t: Blues in My Heart at the Savoy and the guitar players watching
1.s: Danny describes Carter's well-rehearsed charts at the Savoy and how guitarists watched him until Charlie Christian and Jimmy Shirley changed things.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: He's just like that. He's gonna blow all the saxophone... He's gonna play... [SINGS REFRAIN OF "BLUES IN MY HEART"] "Blues In The Night." No, no....

1.t: Lucky Fowler, the Gaslight Club banjo job and Keg Johnson's cameras
1.s: Danny sent Lucky Fowler to the Gaslight Club banjo job and lent him a banjo, and Milt recalls Keg Johnson's passion for cameras.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: A guy called me, Milt Mackler(?), who was a friend of mine, who I used to go in the Village and hang out with -- a White boy. He was a friend of the guy that owned the Gaslight Club, the manager. I can't think of that man's name. He said, "Danny, I've got a good job for you." I said, "What is…

1.t: Cab's search for the greatest guitar player
1.s: Cab kept track of what musicians said about guitarists, but Truehart would not leave Chick Webb and Bobby Johnson would not travel.
1.q: You don’t see Cab. Cab is listening. He always had stool pigeons in them big bands. They’re always big-mouth cats in the band, talking about who’s the greatest. The leader don’t have to hear that he is. He hears what the musicians said. Said, “Teddy Bunn’s the greatest guitar player.” “No, Bernard…

1.t: What 'fat chords' are: the three sets of four strings
1.s: Barker explains playing four-string voicings for volume rather than single-string solos.
1.q: No just playing. Playing chords. You don’t say “just playing.” You say “playing chords.” It’s something that’s a rhythm thing. You do it, and that fills the band. You don’t leave no open spots.

1.t: The Lion's compliment about knowing when to lay out
1.s: Willie the Lion told Danny he was the one guitarist who knew when to lay out, and describes how the Lion's key shifts could trick accompanists.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: See, the Lion said Jelly Roll couldn't play no piano, you know. Like, the Lion is fantastic. The Lion's playing eight-beat, trick you. The Lion paid me a compliment I'll never forget. He said, "Do you why know I like you, Danny? I like your playing." I said, "Why?" I said, "What about it? I can't…

167.t: Philadelphia blues guitarists: Bobby Leecan and Lonnie Johnson
167.s: Rosenberg names early Philly blues guitarists; Bunn knew Bobby Leecan and says they had playing contests which he always won.
167.ch: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
167.q: Oh, yeah. Him and I had tests together about playing.

167.t: The guitar in the 1930s; playing at the mike with Ellington
167.s: Guitar and tiple groups were unusual, banjo was fading, and with Duke he held the guitar up near the microphone.
167.ch: Spirits of Rhythm and the road in the 1930s
167.q: And the guitar was the leading thing then. And all them over in Honolulu was doing them ukuleles.

167.t: His guitars: Stella, Martin and the Epiphone
167.s: Rosenberg traces photos of round-hole flat-top guitars to the arch-top Epiphone; Bunn says he played whichever guitar sounded best.
167.q: Well, I wasn't using no electric guitar then at all.

167.s: He played with first two fingers alternating and the thumb on bass strings, and did glisses with thumb or the whole hand.
167.q: You know, the whole hand, come down on the strings.

167.t: Floating over the beat unlike Eddie Lang
167.s: Rosenberg says his playing stood out for floating away from the beat and returning, unlike Eddie Lang; Bunn says that is how his mind went.
167.q: To make it come out right. And I'd catch that beat at the end.

167.t: The guitar's status in the 1930s and forgotten musicians
167.s: He says the guitarist who played best got the work, and laments that good musicians go unheard, himself sidelined by illness.
167.q: To me it is amazing. All these good musicians around here doing nothing. They can't get a break. Why? There's a lot of them around that you don't hear of them no more.

167.t: Guitarists in New York: Eddie Lang compared
167.s: There were few single-string guitarists in New York; he heard Eddie Lang with Crosby and Whiteman and says Lang lacked ideas.
167.ch: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
167.q: players is coming up here lately. You can hear the same thing. They don't have the ideas. If they have it they never use it.

167.t: Playing his first electric guitar, a Gretsch
167.s: He bought a cheap Gretsch electric and describes playing lighter, sustained notes and no feedback problems.
167.ch: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
167.q: Because any time I'd go to a place and they didn't have an electric guitar for me to play, I'd get up close to that mike.

167.t: "Wearyland Blues" with J.C. Higginbotham and how he held notes
167.s: They play the Blue Note record with Higginbotham and Albert Ammons from the mid-1930s; Bunn can only credit his ear and a gift for his held notes.
167.ch: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
167.q: I don't know. That's what's so funny, I don't know. Just a gift, I guess. And I loved music. I loved it but never could read a note. [Sure don't know] Knew how the hell that would happen.

167.t: Working with piano players; no strap; Meade Lux Lewis
167.s: Rosenberg says Bunn's single-string style suits pianists; Bunn knew where the four beats were, and held the guitar with his elbow and no strap.
167.ch: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
167.q: I know where four beats is. How the hell I know that, I don't know. It had to be a gift. I had to stay close to that. You can tell by the way I'm bearing down on it.

167.t: Tuning down a half tone and the heavy-gauge strings
167.s: He tuned his guitar down a half step with medium strings, giving a fat sound while still allowing bends.
167.q: Yeah. Tuned it down a half a tone.

167.t: Why he tuned down: blending with Doug Daniels's tiple
167.s: He began tuning lower to blend with the high tiples, especially Doug's, and debates with Rosenberg whether it was half or whole step.
167.ch: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
167.q: Because he didn't know the key it was in until he changed the notes. He'd get it down to a natural note, he wanted to play it.

167.t: Keeping the guitar heard in Hampton's small group
167.s: Against vibes and piano in Hampton's quartet he used higher notes to be heard.
167.ch: Hampton, Blue Note and the electric guitar
167.q: But I kept it a lot different, because I had them high notes.

167.t: Al Casey and knowing the ropes
167.s: He did not think much of Al Casey, who knew chords but not enough.
167.ch: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
167.q: Yeah. I didn't think too much of him, as far as that's concerned, because he was (inaudible). Heard of him.

259.t: Young Morgan Band and Transcena's banjo test at Spanish Fort
259.s: A story of the boss Transcena sitting by banjo players and firing one, and how Vincent survived by chording up the neck.
259.q: Have you ever worked with the Young Morgan Band? Yeah, yeah. Let me see. Isaiah Martin. Yeah, I used to work with him. He played his band. He played for me. He was playing out at Spanish Post. And you know, old man, Transcena, he could play music too. Transcena, that's the fella who used to run the…

259.t: Ninths in Mexico and with Jack Carey; keeping in practice
259.s: He played ninths in Mexico in 1926 but not with Jack Carey; he has not touched his banjo in a year due to illness.
259.q: So did you play ninths when you were in Mexico? Yeah. Yeah. Well that's 20- That was 1926 I was right there. Yeah. Okay.

259.t: Switching from guitar to banjo and Baton Rouge players
259.s: He started on guitar at about 21-22, stayed on guitar and then banjo, refused to change at first, and mentions rival banjoists, George Foster and a Baton Rouge job lost over Bob Lyons.
259.ch: Baton Rouge, Hill City and family music
259.q: And when did you change the banjo? Let me see. I must have stayed on guitar about five years. And then they, not that long, about two years. And then they come out with the banjo. And I didn't want to change. Me and Janice received. We said we wasn't going to change. And that was the only man I had…

259.t: Early guitar players and Rabbit from James Alley
259.s: He names early guitarists, praises fingerpicker Henry Roy, and describes Rabbit from James Alley who sang and played guitar.
259.q: He said who were some good guitar players before your time? Well, Henry Martin, he was one of the first cups, was the best. Henry Roy, Stonewall, Philip Nicholson, and uh, what's his name? I can't think of his name. I had him landed my tongue. I forgot his name already. Oh yeah, no runs of stow.…

259.t: Putting heads on his own banjo and Bunk Johnson
259.s: He fixed banjo heads himself, sometimes using drum heads, and recalls Bunk driving a float and buying beer.
259.q: You say how about the cover, the cover you made for your banjo? The cover? The head. The head? The head, the head for your banjo. Did I have a cover? No, the head you made for it. You mean could I put them on with a bust? Yeah. You remember I.C. don't you? Yeah. And then Trumpet there. I see, you…

259.t: Lorenzo Staulz, guitarist with a dirty mouth and many women
259.s: Vincent remembers Lorenzo Staulz as a banjo and guitar player who talked dirty and had many women, and tries to recall which band he played in.
259.q: Yeah. He was a dirty fellow. Talk dirty. Yeah, he had the women, 30 women. They'd be crazy about it. Yeah. A towel across his shoulder. What, a towel across his shoulder? Yeah. Why? He used to find him to come get me, you know. He used to ask me what I'm playing. I said, I don't want to tell you…

259.t: Why he played chords instead of picking, and switching to banjo
259.s: Vincent says he was told picking was too light for the band, so he played chords. He moved from guitar to banjo, learning from Professor Boeese.
259.q: Well, he's the one who learned me how to pick banjo, you see. When I was bad, I used to run across him all the time, you know. He's got a ban now, you know.

259.t: Taking the first hot chorus with a rap, and the closing thanks
259.s: Vincent claims to be the first to take a hot chorus on banjo using a double rap, learned from Julius and perfected with a tin pan behind his banjo. The session ends with thanks.
259.q: He said, did anybody take a hot chorus and play it with chords or pick, pick it? I was the first one that took that hot chorus. Was picking or? Wrapping. Wrapping. Yeah. Wrapping. You know, Eddie, not by myself, the whole band stopped. And just the kick-toe and the bass would take a hot. Oh yeah.…

259.t: Guitarist Jesse Jackson and the men in his band
259.s: Vincent remembers Jesse Jackson as a guitarist with plenty of work and names Eddie Scott and others who played in his band.
259.q: Jesse Jackson. He has, huh? Jesse Jackson. Oh, he was a guitar player. You remember him? He used to have a little help in the mouth. He used to get better weight. He used to have two guitars. He said, well, we don't really play, but he would make motion. I think he would play, but he could make…

259.t: Albert French, singer and banjo player
259.s: Vincent talks about Albert French, a singer who played a little banjo and guitar and who he helped bring out.
259.ch: Liberty Band, marriage and the Depression
259.q: I bought him out. He never would forget me. If he got a little three or four piece jar, he'd come lick me up, come and get me, and we'd all play together. Bandra and guitar, you know. And he would sing, you know.

259.t: Ike Morgan, Sam Morgan and the banjo player story
259.s: Vincent says he played with Ike Morgan's band before Mexico, remembers his brother Sam, and tells a story about a banjo player who was fired.
259.q: You said who was in the band then? Let me see. Ask him if he had his brother with him. Did he have his brother with him? No, no he didn't have his brother then. What's the money he's got in? He had a what kind of penny? Andrew. Well that's one I don't know. Ake Martin. That's the one for a kind of.…

137.t: Homemade amplified guitar and the clothes-hanger bridge
137.s: Durham explains rigging an amplifier and mike to his guitar and a clothes-hanger swinging bridge, a few years before factory electric guitars.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: And lean it over. So finally, I figured out a way to get old amplifier, and got a mike and sometimes used to get the little thing, make them up and put them together and that amplifies that on the stage, run it and get it into the guitar, right in the , hook it in the guitar someplace, and that's…

137.t: Resonator guitar and acoustic guitar on Honey Keep Your Mind on Me
137.s: Honey, Keep Your Mind on Me was acoustic; earlier he used a resonator guitar with a tin piece and mike, giving a bottle-like electrified sound.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: Then, maybe hitting a bottle, because those wasn't like the guitars -- they wasn't perfecting it at that time. But it's the same thing, if I'd hook up into this and put this into the guitar and it'd come to the speaker.

137.t: First electric guitar on the Kansas City Six sides
137.s: His first electric guitar came with Bon Bon's Buddies and the Kansas City Six on Hello Little Girl, though instruments were poor then.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: When I got my first -- I never did get a good one with those bands. First time I got an electric guitar was at Bob Barnie's Buddies and in there. Now, those electric guitars --

137.t: Teaching Charlie Christian the downstroke in Oklahoma City
137.s: In 1937 Durham showed Christian in a pool hall how to play single-note downstrokes like a horn, and Christian picked it up in minutes.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: That's what I've been trying to figure out here. James Richmond was in the band, Buster Smith, and that's when Charlie started to playing. And we used to go down to the pool hall every day, James Richmond would follow, on the pool hall, and I was down there,and Charlie Christian came in, you know.…

137.t: Hearing T-Bone Walker with an electric guitar
137.s: He heard T-Bone Walker in the mid 1930s in the South, a showman with an electric guitar playing terrific blues.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: Yeah, it was pretty close there. Hadn't heard anybody else at the particular time. I was with -- I think I was with , I don't know. It was in the '30s.

137.t: The Seattle amplifier story and the guitar players' hour off
137.s: In Seattle, probably 1938, guitar players were given an hour off to hear him with his amplifier, and his amp failed on stage.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: I think that was in the '30s, because at the time, when I was playing, there wasn't anybody playing. I remember that now, because I came from Seattle, Washington, came from Vancouver, B.C. with a girls' band. And I was going to play Seattle, Washington, coming out of Vancouver, B.C. And the way…

137.t: Makers of amplified and resonator guitars
137.s: He names Ampliphone, Gibson, Stella and National resonators and describes the odd sound he got on Battles' records.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: Well, the accoustic guitar was a -- the Stella guitar was one I used on lots of records. Honey, Keep Your Mind on Me, and then I came in with a --

137.t: Floyd Smith and Floyd's Guitar Blues
137.s: He talked Floyd Smith's mother into buying him a $70 guitar in Nebraska; Smith later made the commercial Floyd's Guitar Blues with Andy Kirk.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: The year I was with Charlie Christian, two months later, we went to Nebraska, and Floyd didn't own a guitar. But he could play a little. And I say, I'm leaving

137.t: Steel guitar and T-Bone Walker's style
137.s: Smith used a steel guitar; Durham says T-Bone Walker was early, with gimmicks, strong bass strings and a jazzy blues swing.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: He was unready, when I heard him, what he was playing then. We didn't know to appreciate it. It's the same thing now today. He had guts and everything in it.

137.t: Joining Moten: guitar and trombone, arranging from the start
137.s: With Moten he alternated trombone and guitar, mostly soloing on guitar, and began arranging immediately; Basie came in about the same time.
137.ch: Moten band, arranging and the guitar
137.q: Yeah, with all the bands, one to another. We play one awhile, and if it's something I like, I'll switch to guitar in most of the arrangements.

137.t: Blue Devils musicians join Moten and the band grows
137.s: Many Blue Devils joined Moten for big pay; the brass grew from three to six, reeds from three to four, and the banjo gave way to guitar and Freddie Green.
137.ch: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
137.q: when I came in, then that made four of us. Then when Lips came in, that made five. Then they added another trumpet, it made six.

92.t: Charlie Christian, Minton's and the Leonard Feather label
92.s: Collins insists he never tried to play like Charlie Christian, recalls hearing him at Minton's and meeting him at Monroe's Uptown House, and objects to being labeled Christian-inspired.
92.q: And I just always heard like this, you know. So as I say, it was just a gift, I guess, you know. But coming back to Charlie Christian, I heard Dizzy say -- Dizzy's the only one who really tells the truth about -- I don't say tell the truth. Who really is aware what happened. I never tried

92.s: Floyd Smith got a little attention, but Christian's electric guitar made people aware of the instrument.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: Well, Floyd Smith was with Andy Kirk's Crook's band. He was getting a little acclaim. But Christian came along, and with his electric guitar and that --

92.t: Getting Charlie Christian's electric guitar through Mike Bryan; Eddie Durham
92.s: He recommended Mike Bryan for Benny Goodman's band, and Bryan gave him Christian's guitar and amplifier, his first electric; he notes Eddie Durham amplified guitar before Christian.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: But any way, this was Kelly's Stables then, and Leonard was coming around then and Georgia All, so now here we go. Benny Goodman had Charlie with him at this time. This

92.t: Eddie Durham, Charlie Christian and Oscar Moore
92.s: He credits Durham as an early guitarist and Christian's exciting style, but says Oscar Moore thought like him harmonically before quitting playing.
92.ch: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
92.q: In jazz, well I think that Eddy Durham in my opinion was one of the early ones. And then came Charlie Christian. And there is a guitarist that we just haven't mentioned at all, and I think that in his way -- he was as great as Charlie, but in a different way. Oscar Moore. Oscar Moore was a great…

92.t: Tal Farlow, Wes Montgomery, Joe Pass and other guitarists
92.s: Collins calls Wes Montgomery the most lyrical guitarist and lists Joe Pass, Pat Martino, Lee Ritenour and Howard Roberts.
92.ch: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
92.q: After Charlie I think Tal Farlow came through with bebop. Playing. And I think one of the great innovators of our time, and who was Wes Montgomery. Wes Montgomery in my estimation was one of the most lyrical guitarists I've ever heard. That includes everybody. He came closer to having it all as far…

92.t: Guitar heritage: Eddie Durham, trombonists playing guitar, Christian's sources
92.s: The first black guitarist who influenced him was Eddie Durham, a trombonist, and he urges young guitarists to ask who influenced Christian.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: But, as I said, this is to show you how these things go right down the line. So that is where it all began, you know, and I think that they should kind of check back, you know, and -- see, now, as I told you, the first black guitarist that I heard, that really should I say influenced me was Eddie…

92.t: Recommending Mike Bryan to Goodman and receiving Christian's guitar
92.s: Collins recommended Bryan for Goodman, who got Christian's Gibson and amp, then gave them to Collins, causing nightly arguments with Roy.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: And Mike made the audition and got the job. In the meantime Charlie Christian was the featured guitarist, and consequently Mike and Charlie became very good friends, and Charlie Christian gave Mike an electric guitar, and an amplifier, that Gibson had given him. But they were giving Charlie quite a…

92.t: Gillespie: Collins in Benny Carter's 1942 band and as a major guitar voice
92.s: They met around 1937 and worked together in Carter's 1942 band; before Christian, Collins was the guitar player.
92.ch: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
92.q: Well, he made records with me and we worked together in 1942 with Benny Carter and that was a great experience too because we had two -- three of the foremost exponents of the instrument like -- three. There was Benny Carter, there was Kenny Clark, there was John and then there was Sonny White, and…

92.s: Gillespie says Christian was a blockbuster but not as deep as Collins, whose rhythm playing changes chords constantly, and he would rather play with him than anyone.
92.ch: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
92.q: Yeah. You see, let me show you the difference in the plane. Christian wasn't as deep as John. You see, Christian was a blockbuster, you know. That area that he came from produced that -- guys that played like that, one note. He'd take one note and run you crazy, you know, Charley Christian, and…

92.t: Gillespie on Collins the studious one and his advanced chords
92.s: Gillespie says Collins, before Charlie Christian, was always working out variations and chords, and was more advanced musically than the young Gillespie.
92.ch: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
92.q: Well, before that time I'd never been closely associated with any guitar player. Well before I met John I hadn't been closely associated with any guitar players, you know, with the exception of -- well before I met Charley Christian I met John Collins and John Collins was always the studious one.…

248.t: Best guitar players and the mandolin contest
248.s: Philip Nickerson and Frank Landry were top guitarists; Dawson won a mandolin contest in the French Quarter.

248.t: Stale Bread, mandolin and banjo players, Tom Denton
248.s: Dawson recalls Stale Bread's white trio in the Irish Channel, rates Big Head Sun the best mandolinist, and says Tom Denton played banjo with the Pelican band.
248.ch: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
248.q: Yeah he's a white boy. He was from the front of town. They had a little trio I believe, a little bunch there he's playing.

248.t: Jules Batiste, Johnny St. Cyr and playing with Robichaux
248.s: Dawson knew of Jules Batiste, praises guitarist Johnny St. Cyr, and says he played guitar in John Robichaux's full band before St. Cyr did.
248.ch: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
248.q: Oh, Jules Batiste. I heard of him, but that's been nice, a good while now. Yeah. Johnny St. Cyr used to play with him. Johnny St. Cyr was, uh... Was a guitar player too. A fine guitar player too. Yeah. Johnny St. Cyr was... Well, he complimented. He played with Brobyshire's band too, used to... He…

248.t: Dawson's first mandolin, turtle shell and rosewood
248.s: Dawson shows Allen his old mandolin, his first instrument, which is inlaid with tortoise shell and ivory, and talk turns to an old photograph at age 23.
248.ch: Hippolyte Charles, the bass and other bands
248.q: You think you could fly in that picture? What? What guitar? You know, me standing up... Huh? Me standing up with the guitar... with the band. With my mustache and I...

248.t: Spanish-style guitar played with a knife
248.s: Dawson explains Spanish tuning and playing the guitar with a knife, and how two guitars complemented the violin lead.
248.q: It's the only one they want to play, uh, say like they want to play like Spanish style, you know, they, they put a, uh, I call it a capotash, you know, a mute. Mm-hmm. And just take your knife and, you know, you could take your knife and, and, and, and play it like that on your lap, you see, and…

248.t: Walter Preston's band at Tom Anderson's, and the guitarist Snow
248.s: Walter Preston, Tom Brown, Charlie Washington and Snow played mandolin and guitars at Tom Anderson's and the halfway house; Dawson sometimes played bass, and the talk wanders into nose candy.
248.ch: The district underworld and street musicians
248.q: Well, he, he played with that, it wasn't such a big band, it was just about three or four pieces, or five pieces, I think it was Walter Preston, Tom Brown, uh, Charlie Washington, and, uh, let's see, what's that guy named, uh, I can't think of the bass player. But anyway, sometimes I used to play…

248.t: Chicken Banks, Professor Young and the freelance bass man
248.s: Dawson identifies Chicken (Arthur) Banks as a casual mandolin and guitar player, mentions Professor Young on violin with Clem, and explains Pickaninny played only short bands.
248.ch: String bands, serenading and violin players
248.q: He never, he used to use a violin, yeah, he had a violin. Mm-hmm. The, uh, had the old man from, uh, uh, Donisonville, Professor Young.

248.t: Guitar finger-picking, embouchures and reading music
248.s: Dawson discusses Frank Landry's and Philip Nickerson's guitar styles, finger-picking and beats, the cornetist with his tongue showing, his two bass lessons, and his limited sight reading.
248.q: How did he tune it? He used to pick the guitar most, you see, but he could play rap, he could play a second, a complement. He didn't use a pick? Yeah, he had to use a pick. Yeah, but could he play with his fingers? Top of it. Yeah, he'd play with his fingers. He could take, he'd play solos, take…

876.t: Role of the guitar in a rhythm section
876.s: St. Cyr says the guitar gives a dance orchestra snap and is its foundation; the best three-rhythm setup is bass, drums and guitar, as in the old New Orleans bands.
876.q: Well, the guitar is a rhythm instrument, and it has a tendency to give a dance orchestra some snap. It gives a regular snap, I mean, it's sort of the foundation to an orchestra.

876.t: Banjo versus guitar and tenor banjo tuning
876.s: St. Cyr advises banjo for what the public wants but prefers guitar, which was New Orleans' foundation; costs and tenor and plectrum banjo tuning.
876.q: Well, I'd advise banjo because it's what the public wants. The music-loving public in a dance orchestra, they like the banjo in preference of guitar. But for myself, I prefer the guitar.

876.t: His own instruments: the Martin and the Gretsch
876.s: The guitar he bought in St. Louis, the Martin on Jelly Roll Morton sessions, and his Gretsch from 1932.
876.q: I just wanted a few. There's a good guitar as you can play. I played Martin. Martin is a very good guitar. In fact it was the Tops at one time. Fess had one, he said he liked the tone. They're very good. It's a very thin material. Then Fess got a fancy Gibson with the big sound holes like the…

876.t: Guitar construction: sound holes, glued bridges, Nick Lucas
876.s: Discussion of round sound holes versus f-holes, loose bridges in damp weather, Nick Lucas's guitar, and shallow thin-bodied tone.
876.q: those clef holes. You like that round hole. Yeah, round hole. I mean you tested it and it says so too. I don't think about a guitar. Yeah, they are much louder. They have a bigger tone. Yeah bigger tone. I might put it throughout the sound more than those clef holes.

876.t: Strings and picks he makes himself
876.s: His preferred Gibson and wrapped-G strings, and the thick blunt picks he makes from toothbrush handles or comb backs.
876.q: Well, they used to have the first three strings, the E, B, and G were steel, all steel. But now you have the rap G, the G is rap as well as the bass strings. And I always use rap G, I like them. Yeah. Yeah. I like the tone of them.

876.t: Ernest McLean and the guitar as soloist
876.s: He praises young Ernest McLean's single-note technique, though not as a rhythm man, and would feature him as soloist.
876.q: He's a guitar player, he has, and a single note technician. And I've heard he's not very much as a chord man in a band. But man, he has technique on the single note man. And he makes chords so far as the number he's playing it goes. But I mean for a rhythm man in a band, he's not much a rhythm man.…

876.t: Black diamond strings, Gibson strings and amplified guitars
876.s: History of wrapped strings, why Gibsons last longer, his preference for volume, and why a good acoustic guitar is best.
876.q: And later they came out with what they called a wrap G. It was wrapped just like the base strings, too. So, you had only two all steel strings on it. This was the first and second. And the black diamond was a very popular string at that time. Yeah. But since then, the Gibson has come out with…

876.t: Instrument-making and the best guitarists, Lorenzo Staulz and Willie Santiago
876.s: St. Cyr made guitar parts for friends; he rates Lorenzo Staulz and himself uptown, and Joe Brooks and Willie Santiago downtown.
876.q: I made a set of little, uh, Badger-Malentong, Bret Masley picture there. Yeah. I made the neck for that. Well, you did have that.

270.t: One of the first Black players with an electric guitar
270.s: He says he was among the first Black musicians with an electric guitar, played it on the boat band in New Orleans.
270.q: Yeah. Well, other fellas came after, they weren't safe that way. But they had a lot of white musicians had an electric guitar. Because I was dealing with the wheel line from way back then, in the late 20s and all through the 30s and things like that, up to today.

270.s: Sayles praises John Marrero as a fine banjoist who composed and left for New York, and remembers Lawrence Marrero in a Tuxedo band.
270.q: Well, John Marrero was a fine banjo player. I remember him when he played with, uh, the Bay Rizley band, which Celestine was the trumpet player. Mm-hmm. Emma Barrett was the piano player. Uh, uh, Simon was the bass player. And, uh, uh, Paul Barberin was the clarinet and saxophone player. And, uh, I…

270.t: Best banjo players of the day
270.s: Sayles names John Marrero as the best banjoist and lists others of the 1930s, including Percy Sevier and Randy Hall.
270.q: John was the best, yeah. And I had another fellow player with Sidney Desby named Percy Sevier. Well, he wasn't playing so much when he came, but after he had been around, he got to be a very good banjo player too. Then we were like, around in the mid-30s, we had Homer Eugene, we had Randy Hall, and…

270.s: He used a Vega, then bought a Paramount tenor banjo for $375 on the Marable boat; he never played five-string.
270.q: Well, I have a Viga banjo. I was using the Viga banjo then, but when I got on the boat with Fate, well, I was making pretty good money and I bought me a Paramount, and I remember that was a $375 banjo in those days.

270.t: One Eye Babe's gut bucket band, Sam Red Allen and fingerpicked guitar
270.s: Small gut-bucket bands played at the Pelican with One Eye Babe on bass and his son on banjo, and Sayles remembers a guitarist who played blues with his fingers.
270.ch: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
270.q: Well they could, but he stuck most of the music. They always did, stuck most of the music. Like I said, the band on the Pelican, we had music, but we had head numbers we did and everything, yeah. Now, and we'll get back to the same thing on the Pelican. And those three and four piece bands they…

270.t: Fingerstyle guitar: his father's technique and Guitar Slim today
270.s: His father played a six-string guitar without a pick or thumb pick; Sayles says Guitar Slim and others now play rock and roll and blues with fingers.
270.ch: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
270.q: Well that's where my daddy played guitar. He never used a pick. He never used a pick? No, my daddy played with his fingers. And he had a rhythmic stroke and in fact he couldn't play with a pick. He tried, he just couldn't play. That's the way he learned how to play.

270.t: Guitar-banjo and tenor banjo tunings in the old bands
270.s: Early banjoists such as Johnny St. Cyr and Lorenzo Starr used a banjo-guitar before the tenor banjo became popular; he also notes the Pelican band's fame, and Ridgley's move toward Suburban Garden.
270.ch: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
270.q: Well I can tell you about that. When the banjo, now when they had banjos in the band like I said, they were using the guitar banjo. Because Johnny, not only Johnny's sincere, there was a couple of other guys around there. A fellow named Lorenzo Starr. They used a banjo guitar. In fact like I said…

385.t: Why he went electric: Eddie Bell's guitar and Charlie Christian
385.s: He wanted to be heard, got an electric four-string, and was changed by hearing Charlie Christian and the amplifier sound.
385.ch: California, Cats and the Fiddle, the Tatum trio
385.q: Eddie Bell ... finally found me a guitar, a four string guitar, I don't know where he got it from but it was electric. I think he made it, I'm not sure. I know it was no more. It was a Gibson. ... they owned a store on 48th St, and Broadway...

385.t: Guitar influences and the Harlem Highlanders
385.s: He names guitarists he learned from, especially Snags Allen of the Harlem Highlanders, a kilted singing and dancing act.
385.ch: California, Cats and the Fiddle, the Tatum trio
385.q: 466 Snags Allen, they had a heck of a group called the Harlem Highlanders. And you never seen nothin like that. I tried to revive it a few years later. If they had the right manager, the boy it was a million dollar act. All dressed in kilts. And they could dance, sing, I played piano for them at…

385.t: New York jam sessions; Charlie Christian plays his four-string guitar
385.s: At Clark Monroe's and Morton's he was learning among great players, and Charlie Christian once took his guitar and played it.
385.ch: California, Cats and the Fiddle, the Tatum trio
385.q: ... I was just learning how to play -- I used to go down to Clark-Monroe's, told, Wilson used to be there. All the great guys used to come there. I had in my mind to play ... they asked me --- whisper it in my ear, say "hey man, look I'm gonna play somethin' here so you lay out, hear?" That musta…

385.t: Oscar Moore and Floyd Smith as guitarists
385.s: He remembers Oscar Moore and Floyd Smith; he heard Smith rehearse and met him much later in Atlantic City but was not influenced by him.
385.ch: Three Deuces and 52nd Street with Tatum
385.q: --- Oscar Moore, excellent guitar player --- Floyd Smith was an excellent guitar player. He was with Andy Kirk a long time. I got in trouble trying to play his blues. learn how to play his blues ---

385.t: Soft Winds and other Christian tunes
385.s: He remembers only Soft Winds from the titles and explains that Christian played what he would have played.
385.ch: Three Deuces and 52nd Street with Tatum
385.q: Soft winds is the only one I could remember. Like I said, I liked all of Charlie Christian's things. Because he played what I would play. He was just thinking ahead of me. I'd say 'Gee, whiz, man. That's what I was going to play.' ... But I'm probably just talking to hear myself talk. He was…

385.t: Pioneer electric guitarist: parallel with Christian
385.s: He says another guitarist played banjo-tuned chords, and he was playing runs before hearing Christian with Goodman.
385.q: That's possibly true because when the electric guitar first came out -- I wasn't no pioneer -- another fella I think I told you -- he had a four string but it was tuned like a banjo, and he just played pretty chords. But I just wanted to play runs --

385.t: Charlie Byrd, Wes Montgomery, and being imitated
385.s: He praises Charlie Byrd's blues playing and Wes Montgomery's octaves, and says being copied is a credit.
385.ch: Chords, recordings and his own groups
385.q: ... Charlie Byrd, he is a great friend of mine. And he's a great guitarist, a lot of people don't know Charlie Byrd can play just about any type of jazz and latin music that there is. He's one of the few cats that can play those slow dragged-out blues. Cause we did it. We worked together several…

309.t: Loudest banjo player in the city
309.s: Julius says he is called the loudest banjo player and his father taught him his way; tone is about strokes, not strength.
309.q: Well, I am, they all tell me everywhere that I'm the loudest fan here player in the city. Which I go along with them. Because, my daddy taught me a certain way.

309.t: Father's violin and the rattlesnake rattlers
309.s: His father put two dried rattlesnake rattlers in his old violin to boost its sound, and Julius wishes he had it.
309.q: You're telling us about his violin. Well, my daddy had a violin, and, uh, no violin he had. The people that gave him this other violin, they said it was 150 years old. It had a good sound, it was a wonderful instrument. The, the weight of it, you know, showed how much, uh, and, uh, someone told my…

309.t: A banjo from the Sosche family who played trumpet with his father
309.s: Julius owns a Vega banjo from a man who played with his father; Joseph and Edgar Sosche played trumpet in the band.
309.q: Just to look at it. I haven't even had a head put in it. It's interesting about that long. But it's, uh, it's a vega, dick? Oh, really? It's a vega, yeah.

309.t: Banjo and guitar duets and switching chords between instruments
309.s: They talk about a duo on television and Julius explains how banjo and guitar chords differ and confuse his playing.
309.q: It's just like if the guitar would make E flat. The banjo would make E flat. The guitar would make E flat minor. The banjo would make E flat minor, but those chords are different. That's what complicates me sometimes. When I play, if I play tonight with my guitar, and I make an E flat 7 or a 9th or…

309.t: Getting his first banjo and why old instruments sound better
309.s: He tried every instrument at home but wanted a banjo; his father's friend got him one for fifty dollars, and he prefers old banjos and calfskin heads.
309.q: I say didn't really switch. Because I always wanted to play banjo. Well, my daddy didn't have a banjo. He had every instrument in the house for the banjo. It's like Sybeth used to play trampons. Slide trampons used to play that too. And, uh, nah, I tried every instrument in the house. But I still…

309.s: With Cap on mandolin leading the melody and Sylvester on bass, Julius played only chords and no solos.
309.ch: Early music and bands on the coast
309.q: No, he'd be playing single notes. Playing the melody or variation? Melody, play the melody, I don't know. Oh, I see. I mean, just like he was playing the sax, just the way he used to play his, uh, the mandolin. And, uh, I mean, he would lead every number. I see. Mm-hmm. He didn't, uh, then, that's…

215.t: Hearing John play George Barnes's arrangement
215.s: Rowe plays a recording in which John Pizzarelli uses Barnes's arrangement and a banjo-derived wrist technique learned from the uncles.
215.q: Well that’s what it’s from. You know John studied banjo with my uncles, and they had this wrist thing going, so you apply it to guitar, that’s what happens.

215.t: Guitars Unlimited and the west coast sound
215.s: Bucky identifies a west coast five-guitar record, likening Tommy Tedesco to Tony Mottola of the west coast.
215.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah. Tedesco is the Tony Mottola of the west coast.

215.s: No amps in his youth, getting his first amp in high school, uncles' acoustic bands, and Wayne Wright sounding great unplugged on Long Island.
215.q: Oh there weren’t any amps. We didn’t have amps. We didn’t have amplifiers yet. We’d sit and hit those strings like there was no tomorrow. I didn’t get an amp until I was like second or third year in high school. And then I played so loud that the bandleader told me to shut up.

215.t: The importance of rhythm guitar and playing without a stand
215.s: Bucky says rhythm guitar is what dancers feel in a big band, and that he needs no music stand.
215.q: Yeah, that’s the whole ball game. I think that’s the most important thing in any big band was the rhythm guitar. That’s what the people danced to.

215.t: Playing a seven-string guitar after George Van Eps
215.s: Pizzarelli explains getting a seven-string Gretsch after hearing Van Eps, and other extra-string and tuning variations.
215.q: No I’ve had that for quite a while now you know, thanks to George Van Eps, a seven string, since ‘68, ‘69 I think, that’s when I started with it.

215.t: Playing the rock and roll guitar sound
215.s: Bucky describes the high electric sound and the muffled wrist-muting technique used on rock dates.
215.ch: Session stories and why he was hired
215.q: Well we knew it was a different kind of sound. You had a guitar with a high pitch electric sound, real high. You knew how to do it. Sometimes we’d go on a date and we’d all make up a thing. One would do [scats] with your wrist on the strings, you get a real muffled sound. That was the most popular…

917.t: Double-time guitar raps and teaching Walter Nelson
917.s: Keppard's double raps on the guitar, shown to Walter Nelson in front of Picou; it is all in the wrist.
917.q: I believe I done showed you, because I done showed, I believe I have, totally right, just like I said, we all have a guess. Let's make, they have rubbers on a passel, you know? Yeah, were you the only one? I believe sometime back I told you about it, that I, that I has taken plaids, and they got…

917.t: Early guitar playing and an electric guitar anecdote
917.s: Straight four beats in older bands versus double raps; an electric guitar anecdote; piano left-hand comparison; an improvised tune.
917.q: Well, I'll tell you. Some of them, you see, like I was telling a fella the other day, I say, you know, he said, what's the name of that guitar? I said, well, this is a, that's that stupid. So that's the way, he said, what kind of, he said, well, what you playing? I said, this is what they call a…

917.t: Straight time versus double raps, and an improvised tune
917.s: Straight four beats in older bands versus double raps; an electric guitar anecdote; piano left-hand comparison; an improvised tune.
917.q: Well, they, they, they, they're playing straight. Like that. Oh, I want a bad lead. See the bad lead? Same with the voice of singing. Yeah. See, that's the way they just give that right straight beat. That's straight beat. And that's better. You know, it's better. But of course, when some of them…

917.t: Frank Ducey's band and other old-timers
917.s: Keppard names sidemen who played with Frank Ducey and Jack Carey, and a still-active old timer, then returns to playing guitar after 1917.
917.q: oh, there's Danny Lewis, he would play bass with Frank Ducey, see, Frank Ducey, and then comes, uh, Jack Kerrig, he used to play with him, well, they had this little fella, they, he, he's a little sharp fella, they had, but he, he's still playing yet, and they call him, uh, Chester's artist,

917.t: Freddie on mandolin and accordion; Manuel Manetta
917.s: Freddie played a little mandolin and the squeeze-box accordion but not in bands; Manuel Manetta is mentioned as a friend.
917.q: Then he played on the mandolin a little bit, but he wasn't playing with no band with the mandolin. But he could play. And he also was playing card then. I guess you know something about the card, Mr. Roussel. Sure. That card with that pull out and push in. The squeeze box. And then Manuel Manetta…

474.t: Working the Silver Street with Cheek and George Lewis; moving to guitar
474.s: Jones worked at the Silver Street in Cheek's band with George Lewis; he put down banjo when guitar became popular.
474.ch: New Orleans bands: Cheek, Parker, Morgan
474.q: Yeah, I'll tell you about it. I used to work at the Silver Street. Listen to this. Yeah. With Cheek as the band leader. Mm-hmm. George Lewis on clarinet. Mm-hmm. Manny Gabriel on saxophone. Now it's been so long I forgot who was on the drum. But I used to work at the Silver Street. That was down in…

474.t: Mandolin players and street guitarist Bobo
474.s: The only mandolin player he knew, and Bobo, a street guitarist with thumb and finger picks.
474.q: He didn't play with nobody but him and uh, him and uh, him and uh, Claiborne's brother. Yeah man. Claiborne and his brother couldn't get along though. The one we called Jill. What did he play? The bass player. Mandolin and bass and a drummer.

474.t: Manuel Sayles, Pete Sayles and the banjo chair
474.s: Banjoists in Sidney Desvigne's and Clyde Kerr's bands, and Jones's succession.
474.ch: Hometown ties, community and favorite players
474.q: Yeah, but I was a Christian after, in 1935 at the Holy Ghost. Oh, did you know sales up the country? In Donalvilleville? No, no, I met, I met, I met Manuel Sells playing with Sidney Desmond. Manuel Sells at this time was living up here. Yeah. He always did live up here.

474.s: Banjoists he admired and Johnny St. Cyr and Rene Hall on guitar.
474.ch: Hometown ties, community and favorite players
474.q: Well, when I first started Kimball. Kimball was all over the country, you know, the first time I heard Kimball, another fellow from Donaldsonville by the name of Clarence Ellis. Never heard of him? Never. He used to call himself Duke Ellis. He played in the deluxe band in Baton Rouge. Duke Ellis?…

474.s: Lemon, who played guitar, banjo and ukulele, gambled for a living, and played over the phone.
474.q: Oh Lemon, when I met, I met Lemon in a race in Louisiana. I met with a guitar. Yeah, he told me he played guitar and banjo.

261.t: John Marrero and Puy Saville banjo rivalry
261.s: Verrett recalls Marrero and Saville, from Natchez, cutting heads at the Pelican and heard from the Music Box.
261.q: Well I heard him. He was a good banjo player too. John Marrero, he was a good man. And him, I heard him. Like I told you, this guy, a banjo player, Pujic Saville. Oh yeah, I heard George Dino talk about him.

261.t: His banjo, the plastic head and a mute behind the bridge
261.s: Talk about his banjo, Peterson fitting a plastic head, tailpieces, and the softer tone from a mute.
261.q: It doesn't get soft. No, no, it don't get soft. You play on the outside, like I play a lot on the outside. It don't... It don't get on. Uh-huh. It gets... It don't soften it up. It's wet, yeah. Yeah.

261.t: Vega banjos and Emile Riley's banjo contest
261.s: Verrett praises the Vega's tone, recalls an Annunciation Square banjo contest, and says where Emmy O'Reilly lives.
261.q: See, he told me to get them one. His is straight, so he ain't got no pressure on the head. Because the banjo he got is a real good banjo. A vega, you can't beat him for tone. That's the best. Kimmel had a $500, $400 paramount, gold, and I don't know if you know, Emmy O'Reilly.

261.t: His Gibson guitar, playing single, and banjo versus guitar in Dixieland
261.s: Verrett discusses his Gibson, solo jobs and pay, and why banjo suits Dixieland better than guitar.
261.q: You used a fast dominant one. Yeah, I had this, but a pickup went bad on. Pickups, it's got to go through a war line with a pickup. Come on, you see? Yeah, it's a big Gibson. It's gone. It's gone. It's gone. There's no effects. Maybe the microphone probably. Well, I called them. I asked them. I…

261.t: Banjo rather than guitar when he started
261.s: Everyone played banjo when Verrett was young, and music stores stocked the best banjos.
261.q: Oh, when I started, that's what they're playing. That's why I like it. Everybody was playing? Yeah, it was banjo. No guitar, it was banjo, see? Everywhere you go, it was banjo, I mean, and they was playing. That's why I said, well, I want to take banjo, and banjo's selling me. I mean, all the music…

432.t: Dave Jones at 225, Chinatown, Celestin and Ridgley, and the stolen banjo
432.s: He names the 225 band lineup, building a name at Chinatown, moving among Celestin and Ridgley, and how friends stole his banjo to force him onto guitar.
432.q: I started organizing my combos. I was working down in the old district down there at uh, 225 with David Jones. Well it was Elric Kuyfer on trumpet. And uh, Boyd Millett playing piano at that time. Henry Russell.

432.t: Banjo or guitar on recordings; jobs with Kid Howard and Morgan
432.s: They sort out which instrument he played on certain tapes and who was on jobs with Kid Howard and Andrew Morgan.
432.q: Yeah I read up there with Howard and what's his name? Abbey Williams? Abbey Howard and what's this guy's name? Morgan, you know, Andrew Morgan. And Handy too was there wasn't it? That sometimes but mostly it was Morgan and Kit Howard.

432.t: Switching to guitar in 1943-44 and bringing an amplifier
432.s: He switched to guitar in 1943 or 44, and at Parisian Gardens Big Joe told him to bring his amplifier despite the pianist's objections.
432.q: No. I was working down there with John Patterson and they told me don't use an amplifier with the guitar so if I'm making bad chords.

432.s: He says he always used an amplifier after the Parisian Gardens job.
432.q: know down there, with Shelken and them used to play. But other than that I had. You always played with the ball. Yeah. Well I was playing with the amplifier. I worked with the amplifier from there on. You see what I had a question. Yeah I want to know about when you played with Beat Lala. You…

432.t: Playing guitar with Sheik Colar in the 1950s
432.s: He recalls jobs with Sheik and Henry Russ and not playing at Preservation Hall.
432.q: We was back there with a group and they had a hole in the head, Walter, that boy we used to be with Fat Domino, his daddy. You know Walter. Yeah, Papoosh. Papoosh used to, Daddy used to be across the street. And Henry was down there with his brothers, never did get along with them brothers. You…

197.t: Boat band personnel and guitar versus banjo
197.s: Names the players on the Piron boat band, discusses guitar without amplifier, preference for guitar or banjo, his trumpet and family instruments.
197.q: During that time, Leo Dejean, Joe Phillips, Eddie Pearson. Oh, yeah. And Eddie Pearson. And it was trombone. And saxophone was Louis Cartrell, Oscar Rouson, and Elliot Taylor. On the drums was Sidney Montague, Booker, Booker Washington on bass, Lewis Gibbons on piano, and I was playing the straight…

197.t: Banjo players he admired when learning
197.s: Names the good banjoists of his youth, Preston, Thomas, Kimball, Rene Hall, Danny Barker and others.
197.q: Well, they had some real good banjo players after I started learning how to play banjo. Because during that time, Walter Preston, Kit Thomas, and Bocas, they were the kind of banjo players that the fellas started playing a little later on. Because the fellas a little later on started playing the…

197.s: Banjo was already popular when he started; earlier guitar; Marrero praised.
197.q: Well, yeah, I understood because I heard his record by Louis Armstrong with his Hot 5 during them times. Johnny Sincere was playing the guitar. They didn't have no banjos then, I don't remember.

197.t: Percy Sevier and other banjo teachers
197.s: Recalls Percy Sevier and other banjoists; guitar took over from banjo; lessons from Kimball, Sayles and Sevier.
197.q: Well, I don't know what happened to him, but during the time he was playing with Sidney Desvins' band, when I heard him.

197.s: No single favorite banjoist; his first cheap banjo, his Vega now, Kimball's costly banjos.
197.q: Well, like I said, during that time, I don't know who could play the best banjo because all of them was good during them times. Just like I said, Irene Lee Hawley was an exceptional good man.

650.t: The Red Book and why he preferred the guitar to violin
650.s: They discuss the Red Book of rags and his reading ability; he says the guitar is the hardest instrument and all others are toys.
650.q: Oh, I used to play a piece of avalanche, you know? Little exercises and things like that. I can pick up now, I figured I'd play it then, but... I put it down a long time. You know, you only see the scene be mechanical to me. I'll leave, I'll take a guitar and lay it down next month, next year, pick…

650.t: His own rags and guitar playing for the recorder

He's quite a band man, Johnny Sincere's, you know. He was quite a guitar. Of course his main way of making his…

896.t: Switching from banjo to guitar and the steel guitar

896.ch: Chris Kelly and the dance halls
896.q: Well I switched from banjo to guitar. I got the guitar in 1943. I got the guitar in 1943. A lot later than you started on banjo. Oh banjo was after I left the violin I jumped on the banjo. Yeah. Yeah that was around 1919. Jumped on the banjo. Yeah right after the war. That's right.

896.t: Banjo versus guitar in the band
896.s: Banjo was the only instrument then; he prefers guitar because it is easier, was self-taught on it, and says modern guitars need amplifiers while the banjo carries in a band.
896.q: Well, the guitars that they have now, they're made especially for the amplifier that you cannot hear them in the band now. So, the banjo, you can hear them in the band. Banjo is kind of imitating a drum.

896.t: Caffrey Darensbourg, the banjoist at the roof garden
896.s: His favorite banjo player was his younger cousin Caffrey Darensbourg, a fast lead player at the roof garden who learned mandolin in their hometown first.
896.q: Did I like to be your best? Yes. Which were the best players? Well, I will tell you. I had a little cousin. He was playing with P. Ron on the roof garden.

896.s: He recalls John Marrero, who played with Papa Celestin, and Russell talks about the Marrero brothers.

896.t: Favorite guitarists after the banjo went out

33.t: Banjo in his early band, George Potter and pianist Frankie Frober

They loved it and they played. That's all. But the original was just five men without any bass. And I always thought that I…

33.s: DeDroit mentions Edna Orman and John Hammond, earning extra for solos, and organist Ray McNamara.
33.q: He played dance music too. Ray was a composer. I think he's a member of VASCAP. He gets a check. Well you recorded one of his tunes. What? Well, I was getting back to the guitar and the banjo.

33.t: Band loyalty, bassist Dan LeBlanc and guitarist Arthur Ponce

And they love their leader in spite of what people think. But they used to try to put me on in lots of ways. I remember…

577.t: Banjo rhythm and the switch to guitar in New York

I mean, I didn't use much amplification on the guitar, I didn't have the pickups on the guitar, they used to get up closer to my guitar. Well, did it sound like a guitar? It sounded more like a guitar than with the…

251.t: Mandolinist Caffrey Darensbourg and the Troy Floyd date

128.s: Many guitarists played around Day Range, some better than he was; blues were scarce then and old songs like Steamboat Bill were played.

128.t: Johnny Dede on banjo and George Ginnon as substitute

786.t: Curly and Willie B with the steel guitar
786.s: Corley recalls jug player Curly and Willie B on steel guitar, with whom he played.

786.s: Corley mentions Roosevelt Stokes and Earl Bell, Frank Stokes's guitar playing, Dan Sane, and one-legged guitarist James Dewberry in St. Louis.

786.q: Well, the reason I lose my thumb, I never play with a pick to do no good. I used to play with my thumb all the time. I get as much out of my thumb as I do a pick. It breaks too many strings.

786.s: Shade says Furry Lewis played bottleneck on John Henry, and explains Vastapol and Spanish tunings.

28.t: Charlie Christian and Oscar Ellman compared
28.s: Butler never heard Charlie Christian live but says Ellman, whom he heard personally, was fantastic and would have excited Christian.
28.ch: Reflections on Paris guitarists and saxophonists
28.q: However, Oscar Ellman, I heard him personally. He is the most fantastic, if he's not, he's still fantastic. Now, you've got some guitar players in Italy who you better be very careful of.

28.t: Hearing Charlie Christian over the BBC
28.s: Drunk on champagne and rum in Europe, Butler was sobered by Christian's guitar on the BBC and felt he affected him like Oscar Ellman.
28.q: You'll hear about him no matter where you at, you'll hear him somewhere, because Charlie Christian, in fact, I'd been drinking champagne and rum which is most dangerous to drink.

28.s: Butler recalls hearing another 'demon' guitarist, Robert Norman, in Norway in the late 1930s.
28.q: So, that's the way it goes. He affected me the same way that Oscar Ulman affected me -- that's how the affect was. That's how the effect was and a guitarist -- Whoh -- I forgot about a Norwegian boy.

237.t: Why banjo players switched to guitar in the early thirties
237.s: Goodwin says the resonator guitar was mellow, better for singers and combos, and banjos were hard to record.
237.q: Well, the guitar began to be amplified -- well, not at the start, see, but they had -- they had a guitar with a steel back on it and it had a resonator on it and it could be heard in small combos.

237.t: Eddie Durham and wishing he played classical guitar
237.s: Goodwin patterned himself on Eddie Durham and would trade everything to be a classical guitarist like Segovia.
237.q: In your opinion, what is the biggest difference between a classical guitar and the jazz guitar? I mean simple now, quick and easy.

237.t: Goodwin's lost banjo and meeting Smith at a Pearson Hall rehearsal
237.s: Goodwin played banjo in Lovett's Dixieland band and met Smith at a rehearsal for a Pearson Hall job; Smith thanks Lovett.

179.t: Playing chords only; banjo was his first instrument

179.s: With Kid Thomas he played guitar and a little banjo; he got rid of both when he quit but kept the first one as a souvenir.

179.t: Favorite banjo and guitar players and mandolinists
179.s: Johnny St. Cyr and Caffrey Darensbourg who took solos; mandolinist Arthur Jefferson, a big man.

627.s: Williams says he picks with two right-hand fingers and uses all of his left, and plays in C, flat E minor and Spanish tunings, sometimes with a knife; cross-note is flat E minor.
627.ch: Williams on guitar technique and prison
627.q: I only have picked with my dog finger, the stomach, which would be one finger in my thumb. But my left hand, I use all of my fingers.

45.t: Good rhythm sections and their players
45.s: Williams names rhythm sections of Henry Martin, Buddy Petit, and Ridgely, and the reading players in the musical bands.
45.q: Well, Henry Martin. That you heard? Well, Henry Martin. He had Lorenzo Stahls, you know, with Laura and you know, see Lorenzo Stahls and Montulli on bass, you know.

188.q: you get more rhythm too for my part I can handle four strings better than I can handle six all kind of rhythm you know up and down twist and everything you see a lot of good a lot of wrist work you see uh like uh I had a plenty of fellas breaking strings trying to tremble low and and the waltz beat…

49.t: Snoozer Hall's tone and Whiteman's St. Charles concert
49.s: He describes Joe Capraro's guitar influences and Snoozer Hall's fiddle tone, then how he pressed Whiteman to play jazz at his concert.

See when I had the band at the roof, Snoozer used to come up there and sit with us, whenever he was in town, you see. He'd come up there and sit there with us…

8.t: Bud Scott and other guitar players
8.s: Bud Scott as the best guitarist of the time, along with others.

8.t: Guitar and banjo versus piano; amplified guitars
8.s: Garland prefers guitar or banjo with violin, bass and drums in the seven-man band, and says amplifiers drown everything.

195.t: The Doughboys' rhythm men and the southwest versus southeast style
195.s: He names banjoist Marvin Montgomery and guitarist Zeke Campbell and sums up his theory that Southwest style spread east. He says southeastern swing was closer to New Orleans.
195.q: well we left uh the rhythm then uh all of us were playing the rhythm section by there in the dough boys now you have extremely competent musicians old land marvin montgomery the banjoist is a terrific terrific guy and uh we had a fine little guitarist as i said the guitar was one of your key men…

195.s: He explains how guitar, bass, banjo and later piano divided the rhythm work. He credits Marvin Montgomery's slurring banjo runs as a model for his own piano style and mentions the banjo's African American origin.

837.t: Guitar versus banjo in early bands; St. Cyr's capo and pick
837.s: Few banjos were in the early bands. Johnny St. Cyr played a homemade six-string guitar with a pencil capo and a toothbrush pick. Players used thumb and index finger, and Souchon's three classical lessons ruined his playing.
837.ch: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
837.q: you know, those different things. Well, I want to say just this, that I remember very few banjos in the band until much, much later. Very few. In fact, I don't remember any in Oliver's band until Johnny St. Cyr began pulling out that homemade six-string guitar of his. And I want to say this, too,…

837.t: Thompson McKay and Snoozer Quinn, the greatest guitarist
837.s: Thompson McKay played plantation-style guitar. Snoozer Quinn is called the best guitarist ever, with vibrato, a violin stunt, and a stint with the Owls at Suburban Gardens.
837.ch: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
837.q: And it just messed me up. I couldn't get that stroke. Now, Thompson McKay, there were two brothers, Percy and Thompson. Percy is one of the vice presidents of the Whitney Bank. Thompson's a consulting engineer in Dallas for one of the very big engineering firms. He was better than Percy and he had…

837.t: Why Souchon prefers banjo to guitar in a band
837.s: He would rather play banjo with a band because it kicks the rhythm along and cannot be turned off the microphone. The old guitar could be heard only near the band.
837.ch: Guitarists and the Pierron and Brown bands
837.q: Well, I personally rather play a banjo with a band. I think it kicks it along much better and they can't turn that damn microphone off like they do when I play a guitar. They can't hear me a damn bit and they're forced to hear me with a banjo. But personally, not only about myself, I think a banjo…

967.s: A Huey Smith record King played on is heard, and he explains his staccato rhythm guitar buried in the mix.

Like you would hear a guitar when you're in the studio recording. And then when you listen at the playback again. Nothing on that's…

967.s: King says the guitar played rhythm support, and that Allen Toussaint kept guitarists from playing hot licks.

639.t: Snoozer Quinn's life and electric guitar
639.s: He gives Quinn's origins, appearance and character, his guitar playing at Werlein's, and his liking for an electric pickup.
639.q: It may have been from Fawcett's when he was born. Yeah. But he was such an awful nice man, too. Such an awful nice fellow. There wasn't a mean thing in him. He never said a mean word about anybody.

639.t: Wiggs records Snoozer Quinn at the TB hospital
639.s: Wiggs tells how he met Quinn through Peck Kelly, Quinn's style, and the difficult platter recording in the hospital that gave 12 sides.

741.s: The Brian Moore, Jim Mapson archtop, and his collection of guitars he keeps playing.

26.t: Playing a duet with Django Reinhardt before a Boston concert
26.s: Greer and Django improvise backstage with brushes on a newspaper and Duke adds an encore.

So we were -- we had about an hour before -- we always got to the place an hour or so, the band would be relaxed. So me and him, he was sitting backstage playing one…

67.t: Meeting but never playing with Django Reinhardt

67.ch: Latin bands, Wilbur DeParis and Goodman

120.t: Meroff the showman and the band's novelty instruments

120.q: No - I must say that I have never worked for such a clever guy as Benny Meroff. He was probably one of the greatest showmen I have ever seen.

120.t: Eddie Condon as a musician and chord man

73.t: Dart's Hall and the visiting big bands

73.t: First night: single-string versus playing rhythm
73.s: He felt like a stranger, tried single-string playing, and was told to keep time; he has played rhythm since.

103.t: Cliff McTyre, Freddie Green and Walter Page's rhythm guitar

I knew the blues singers. I knew the banjo…

103.t: Eddie Durham and the electric guitar
103.s: He praises Eddie Durham as the first to bring the electric guitar into focus, recalls his amplifier being stolen in Baltimore, and Benny Morton's arrival.
103.q: But prior to that time before we added Benny Morton in '37, Eddie Durham had left Jimmy Lunceford and joined us in '37...

174.t: Desdunes spelling and his violin and banjo playing
174.s: Spelling of Desdunes' name, and his skill as violinist but weak banjo playing.
174.q: He's a very good violinist, very good violin player. And I remember this well, he couldn't play that banjo too well, you know. He had one of the big, what do you call it, a plexon with that long neck on.

174.t: Harris Desdunes and his banjo playing

246.t: Banjo and guitar rhythm, fingers versus picks
246.s: Glass explains banjo being used without piano and how guitarists played with fingers, picks or bone.

663.t: Tuning, picks and the twelve-string guitar
663.s: He tunes one way, uses thumb and finger, and played a twelve-string with three strings removed; also mentions Saints and old-time religion.
663.q: Larry Burndes had a twelve string guitar. You know. So, he had twelve strings on it and I took on nine strings. You took nine strings? Right. And left the rest of them in there. And I played with a finger and thumb. Finger and thumb.

663.s: He never played electric guitar, prefers steel-bodied guitars, and has not used a fretless or bottleneck style.
663.q: I used a lot of chalk cross ties. Scraped cardinals.

848.t: Banjo or bass in Celestin's band
848.s: Russell checks whether Kimball played banjo or bass on the Biloxi job and records.

848.s: Banjoist Caffrey with Manuel Perez inspired him; school dances at the Pythian roof garden.

260.t: Nappy on banjo influences: Stale Bread, a riverboat kid, Lou Black
260.s: Nappy says he had no favorite banjo players. He recalls Stale Bread, a young Black banjoist on a boat, and Lou Black of the Rhythm Kings in Chicago as inspirations.

And he sort of inspired me a little. And also this banjo player with the Rhythm Kings. I don't remember his name. Louis Black. Louis Black.…

260.s: Nappy took up electric bass about two and a half years earlier but still uses six-string guitar on record dates. He recalls banjo and guitar both used in New Orleans, with guitar just coming in.
260.q: Oh, about, let's see, about two and a half years ago. Is that right, Ray? Yeah, about that. Yeah, last time we went to Chicago. That's right. I picked it up here. I picked up the amplifier here and I just started to play it.

38.s: Fiddlers moved to banjo; Levy forms a roadhouse trio with Wyatt Houston, Milt Hinton and himself, and they stampede the place.
38.q: Wyatt Houston was one of them that was a classical fiddler that turned to jazz and he really could play it. He played all the Joe Van Nudie stuff. Is that so? And all the Eddie Saw's stuff. 268.t: George Augustine's role in the Sonny South band

268.q: Well at the time, see I don't know whether he was managing the band at the time, that he talked to me or not, but he had something to do with it I know. But he was the original Sonny South. He died too.

268.s: He tried guitar and would have liked the chord style of Charlie Christian.
268.q: Well, I tried the guitar, but I never could make it. I played a few chords on it. I loved guitar, and I wanted to take lessons, but I never did get around to it. But that was my next instrument, if I was, you know, I just loved that instrument, but I never did get around to it.

968.t: Favorite guitar and banjo players of his youth
968.s: He names Willie San Diego, Lloyd Keppard, Lorenzo Stoll, Willie Bonte and Tom Benton, and says his brother John was praised by everyone.
968.q: Well mostly fell there was a lot of guitar players like Willie San Diego. You know Mr. Willie San Diego. Also Mr. Lloyd Kepper. I know your name is Lloyd Kepper. Oh yes. Mr. Lloyd Kepper. A lot of other people I can't think about the name.

968.t: Switch from guitar to banjo and banjo versus guitar
968.s: Guitars were universal around 1910, banjo took over about 1915, and he prefers banjo for its drive; chords are more complex today.
968.q: All of them I've seen they were using guitars that time. That would be 1910 about. That's around 1910 they were all using guitars.

818.s: He played guitar for the last year with Salvaggio and in Blue Parody, then left after four months for Streeman; guitar overtook banjo around 1932.
818.q: Well, because in 1932, guitarists sort of became real popular and banjos started dying down.

818.t: Selling the Paramount banjo and later the guitar
818.s: He regrets trading in his Paramount banjo for $25, and later sold the guitar to bandleader Larry Vecca.

800.q: Johnny used to play a banjo. He died. Johnny? What was his last name? Johnny, uh—Johnny Simon. Johnny Simon? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

284.q: Oh yeah, that's what I played when I went out. You had the electric attachment? Mm-hmm, that's what I played when I was playing with Senior Desvene.

642.s: Rolf reads a review praising Guesnon over Marrero; Guesnon explains his wrist technique that makes the banjo sound like a mandolin.
