54.ch: Bud Scott band instrumentation and repertoire
54.q: I'm more than great. I think I know a couple of boys, they just practically done. They retired now, has little jobs, but they're pretty bright after all. They, they pick up one, you know, sometime, in different places, and, you know, do lots of... They've got pretty good voices, and they memorize…

666.t: Fred Ogden's banjo and Rene Jelpie's string playing
666.s: Fred Ogden played a banjo-mandolin type instrument and Rau, Rene and Monk sometimes played as a string group.
666.q: But he also had a nice sense of humor. He could tell these funny stories that went along with our type of entertainment there. But if I'm not mistaken, Fritz at that time was playing the banjo or some kind of makeshift banjo, banjo mandolin or something, I don't know what the hell they called it. I…

666.t: Rene Jelpie and Monk Smith's guitar styles
666.s: Rene picked self-taught fingerstyle melody and variations, while Monk strummed chords; the interviewer compares this to the early records.
666.q: He would be playing the melody and variations on the melody and everything else. He played it like nobody ever heard before. I agree. And he taught himself. I mean I don't think he ever had a lesson in his life. But he picked it up somewhere along the line and he played it extremely well.

299.s: He names Charlie Christian and Les Paul, and local guitarists Irvin Charles and Homer Eugene; no lessons from them.
299.q: Well on records, during that time, Charlotte Christian for Swing and Les Paul for Technique. Yeah. I mean, that was my two favorite guitar players.

299.t: Guitars, strings of lessons and picking style
299.s: He used Gibson guitars, no electric at first; his father taught him the MacNeil method; he always used the pick.
299.ch: Guitar, recordings and Johnny St. Cyr
299.q: Well, he taught me for, he taught a lot of books and sheet music at times and different other little instrumental solos. Yeah. You know, like that.

300.t: Sonny Handy and the Astoria band with Rene Hall
300.s: Humphrey names the band of Roy Evans, Sonny Handy, Lee Collins, Joe Robichaux and Rene Hall, nicknamed Plectum for his five-string guitar.
300.q: Pastor Sam, Bill told me yesterday. Yeah. I thought it was Bay St. Louis. But now he used to be a heck of a clarinet player. Uh-huh. Then he changed the saxophone, and he got tough with that saxophone. Couldn't nobody beat him right now.

300.s: The men discuss how Rene Hall played the five-string instrument, with a pick, and how he surprised the band with it.
300.q: Yeah. Mm-hmm. And then, when he brought that, uh, that, that long-necked band in there, oh, he had two feet, remember, the boy line there was, you know, Mm-hmm. I saw that he was, uh, making of a outstanding bandit player, they let him, you know, use him, you know, demonstrate. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Man,…

833.t: Declining offers to play clarinet; Boston Penison and the guitar
833.s: He kept the violin a long while, ducked musicians who wanted him, and praises a Baton Rouge guitarist who could imitate a mule.
833.ch: City bands, Johnny Dodds and the bag factory
833.q: No, For a long while after that, I gave it up. And boys used to come here and get me, you know, to play with them, you know. But, uh, not Buddy P.T. That boy is dead. He was buried in the Gerard Cemetery. I forgot his name. But I played with several of them. The trumpet player, was it? Yeah, he…

833.t: Bud Scott of Natchez and the guitarist nicknamed Bud Scott
833.s: Robinson says he patterned his band on Bud Scott's Natchez string bands, never played with him, and nicknamed his guitarist Frank Sheese 'Bud Scott'.
833.q: Or was there a clarinet at that time? Yeah. No clarinet. No clarinet either? No clarinet. Just a cornet, violin, two guitar, and a bass violin. Almost a string band, wasn't it? Two guitar, yeah, yeah, string band. We were petering at this fella, Joe Scott, you know, in Natchez. No. No, I don't…

438.t: Freddie Green technique: the right-hand fingernail
438.s: Rowe and Chirillo discuss Chirillo's writing on Freddie Green and the right-hand index fingernail brushing the strings, which Bucky also explains.
438.q: In this end, right. That’s right. Well Bucky will tell you that too if you really start asking him about different things.

438.t: Freddie Green's role, heavy strings and the sabotaged amp
438.s: Why Freddie Green never soloed: very high action and heavy strings; the story of the band falling apart when his amp was sabotaged.
438.q: Yeah, well it’s — most don’t. It is, it’s a very limiting role. If that’s all I did I’d get, I’d probably go nuts too. Freddie Green was pretty special. I mean you’ve giving a hundred percent all the time, I mean never solo. And why do you think Freddie Green never soloed, because his strings were…

606.t: Schools of jazz guitar: Christian, Django, chord stylists
606.s: Ellis contrasts the Charlie Christian and Django Reinhardt schools and names George Van Eps as the best chord stylist.
606.q: Well the two main stylists I believe would be Charlie Christian and Django Reinhardt. And Charlie is more right in the face, you know bang, just lay it right in there. And Django sort of flirts with it. I don’t mean that negatively. He plays a lot more notes than Charlie would play. And Charlie…

606.t: Charlie Christian and Django as influences
606.s: Charlie Christian was the biggest influence though Ellis never saw him live.
606.q: Absolutely. And Django Rinehardt to some degree, but Charlie was the biggest influence.

579.t: Researching the guitar book: Charlie Christian to roots
579.s: She plans to start with Charlie Christian, Wes Montgomery and George Benson, and dig into early blues and New Orleans guitar, with Freddie Green mentioned.
579.q: Well, yeah, I’m going to do all that. But I know I’m going to begin with Charlie Christian, and I’m going to go from Charlie Christian on to Wes Montgomery, and there are others, Eddie Lang and Oscar Moore in the older crowd. So I mean by now there’s a certain amount I’ve picked up enough to know…

579.t: Joe Williams's group and his guitar playing
579.s: They try to recall Williams's guitarist; Gourse reveals he plays a bit of guitar, which he never mentioned to her.
579.q: Yeah, a little bit. At least a little bit. I don’t know how much. You know writing this whole book he never mentioned to me he played guitar.

906.t: Freddie Green, steady influence and golf
906.s: Freddie Green was retiring and steady, and he and Marshall Royal turned Joe from tennis to golf.
906.q: Oh, what can I tell you about Freddie? He was just a wonderful steady influence going through the band all the time. He was very retiring, you know he never got in the way or showed off or was obvious anywhere, he just was there, pounding away and being sweet and charming.

906.t: Freddie Green's solo, amplifier story and singing
906.s: An anecdote about Freddie's amp being sabotaged, his scat at the start of 'Li'l Darling', and a tape of him singing 'Them There Eyes'.
906.q: At the beginning of “L’il Darling” he goes [scats]. But we’ve got a record of Freddie singing, “Them There Eyes” I think it is. Yes, my cousin Andrew is a great jazz collector, and he sent Joe a tape of Freddie singing years ago. I can’t remember what the occasion was, but he was quite reasonable.…

503.t: Correcting the name: Eddie Durham and the first electric guitar
503.s: Brown and Burrell sort out that Eddie Durham, not Ernie, was the first electric guitarist and helped Charlie Christian.
503.ch: High school, Dizzy and Wayne State
503.q: Yeah, he was the first and he also helped Charlie Christian.

503.t: Charlie Christian, Oscar Moore and Django Reinhardt as guitar influences
503.s: Christian's single lines, Moore's chords and Django's individual sound shaped how he approached the guitar, along with the blues.
503.q: And I heard him playing the guitar and he was the first one to really play, he wasn’t the first one to use an amplifier, he was probably the second one. The trombonist, I can’t think of his name at the moment…Ernie something…he’s also an arranger. You’ll help me with that later, we’ll think of his…

105.t: Why he always keeps a guitar rather than piano
105.s: Replacing cello in the group with Charles Lloyd and Albert Stinson, he explains that guitar's sustain suits his dancing style better than a keyboard.
105.ch: Bebop, band changes and the road
105.q: I found the guitar playing was very conducive to my playing, the sustaining power of the guitar as opposed to keyboard. Keyboard has no sustaining power, you know. The guitar can say (musical sound). He can hold a note for almost two bars -- I mean a sound.

105.t: Working with Benny Carter, country players and meeting Charlie Christian
105.s: Before the army he did gigs with Benny Carter, recorded with guitarists like George Van Eps, and met Charlie Christian through Lee Young.
105.ch: Bebop, band changes and the road
105.q: Yeah. Well no, I didn’t, you know -- hey I recorded with Bonnie Castle, George Van Eps, recorded with -­

451.t: Why Charlie Christian was an epiphany; Solo Flight
451.s: Hall describes the stunning impact of Christian's playing and the Eddie Sauter piece Solo Flight, and says he would not have sat in with such players.
451.q: That’s fascinating. In a way the jazz [type?], ‘cause I told you I did an interview for this guy who works at NYU, up at Barnes & Noble, and he kind of asked me, “Well, what was so good about then?” And I almost said, “Dummy, listen to the goddamn thing. Are you kidding? Of course it got my…

451.t: Django Reinhardt and meeting his son Babik
451.s: Hall talks about Django's injured hand, the Nazi years, a book on Reinhardt and meeting Babik at a festival.
451.q: Yeah, in a certain sense, the exact opposite of Charlie Christian, ‘cause he played flurries of notes, which was remarkable because, as you know, his hand had been seriously injured in a fire ‘cause he grew up in a, I was gonna say a gypsy household, a gypsy camp, or something. And, and during the…

227.t: Why big bands should keep a guitar
227.s: Mandel argues a good rhythm guitarist helps a band like Woody's or Terry Gibbs's Dream Band.
227.ch: Tiny Kahn, radio and Your Show of Shows
227.q: But we didn’t have a guitar and that band needed one, it should’ve, you know we needed a guy like Turk Van Lake or Sam Herman, somebody like that.

227.s: They discuss why bandleaders dropped guitar, how chugging guitarists tied down rhythm sections, and the good players like Freddie Green and Barry Galbraith.
227.ch: Count Basie, Artie Shaw and the soprano experiments
227.q: Same thing, everybody wanted to go with three piece rhythm sections; sort of like Dizzy’s band and Billy Eckstine. Well, in those days most guitar players used to not be a good thing to have. I mean they didn’t play like Freddie Green, they chugged away, like chug, chug, chug, chug and that did tie…

528.s: Brown asks about the 2006 album with John Scofield and Bela Fleck; Tyner cannot recall details.
528.ch: Steinway, Blue Note, awards and wrap-up
528.q: Yeah, I have forgotten the little details. I think Orrin had something to do with that, I think he was the producer on that project.

528.s: Tyner explains he brought a koto back from Japan and used it on Sahara.
528.q: I like the sound of it. It was considered the Japanese piano before they started making pianos themselves. I enjoyed it, and I heard a lot of it when I was in Japan, so it was fascinating. Fooling around with it, I would pluck it. I didn’t study the instrument so I couldn’t say I was going to play…

109.t: Charlie Christian's calm; he fit the new music
109.s: Charlie Christian stayed calm about his sudden success, loved to jam, and found in New York the music he had been looking for.
109.ch: Ella, Charlie Christian and Europe with Hayes
109.q: Yeah. Yeah. Well, he was kind of -- he was very calm about the whole thing. He never got very excited about it. It didn't boil him much.

109.t: T-Bone Walker, Oklahoma City and Charlie's brother
109.s: Dance recalls T-Bone and Charlie learning chords in Oklahoma City and asks if Charlie's brother also had tuberculosis; Clarke cannot say.
109.ch: Ella, Charlie Christian and Europe with Hayes
109.q: I couldn't say that either. Because I met his mother when she came to New York.

106.s: Briggs says Django's brother Joseph played decent solos in clubs but was inspired by and subordinate to Django.
106.ch: Chez Florence, the Hot Club and Django
106.q: No, he never soloed, 'cause probably his brother didn't allow him to solo. But in playing in a cabaret or playing in a place, he soloed --

106.t: Django's ear and his two-finger technique
106.s: Briggs calls Django another Bechet with a wonderful ear who learned tunes by following chords, playing with two fingers while using the paralysed ones to bar.
106.ch: Chez Florence, the Hot Club and Django
106.q: He was another Bechet. He had a wonderful ear. His ear was trained, and you'd hit a chord, and he's got it.

68.t: Charlie Christian in the Towles band
68.s: Tate says Christian already had his mature style, playing saxophone-like lines, and talks about whether he could read.
68.q: Nobody else played like that. He was the first one. He was playing solo and he sounded like saxophone, man. He played all that stuff we played, you know. He -- we'd make something on saxophone, he says, 'Don't be mad if you hear that again,' and we heard it again.

68.t: Basie's piano and Freddie Green's guitar in the rhythm section
68.s: Tate praises Basie as an accompanist who never gets in the way, says Freddie Green is the flavor of the band, and names Steve Jordan as the only player like him.
68.ch: Armstrong, Parker and life inside the Basie band
68.q: Yeah, he was playing much more than now. And I always loved him. I think he's one of the best in the world to play with. He never gets in your way and he's there when you need him. If you need to hear a chord, he knows it. You know, like he feeds you and he never gets in your way. So he is really,…

70.t: Rhythm guitar: Basie's guitar and Clarence Holiday
70.s: Basie's band kept a guitar, which Jackson says adds to a rhythm section; Clarence Holiday was the greatest rhythm guitarist he heard.
70.q: Well, you see, Basie's band is the only one that really kept a guitar, and it's a funny thing. You know, to me a guitar adds something to a rhythm section if it's a good guitar.

70.t: Sam Herman and Barry Galbraith, rhythm guitarists
70.s: Jackson praises Sam Herman with Tommy Dorsey and Barry Galbraith, whom Redman used on every record date, as unsung rhythm guitarists.
70.q: Yes, and to me there's a white boy that is an unsung hero to me as far as playing rhythm guitar is concerned that people don't even talk about him, because he doesn't really play anymore anyway. He's got a copying service now. He's Sam Herman.

641.t: Hearing Roque with Toots; banjoist Skeets and the encore tune
641.s: Joe heard Roque in church dances and loved a banjoist named Skeets who stopped the show with No, No, Nora; Toots mostly led and talked to the crowd.
641.ch: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
641.q: Yes. Whenever he played with any band... A lot of times the Catholic Church would sponsor dances on a Friday night or Saturday night, and Manuel would be playing there with one of the bands, even Toots or Augustin or Tody...

641.t: Bud Scott and which Bud Scott
641.s: They sort out the two banjo players named Bud Scott and Joe rates Bud as the best musician in the Ory band.
641.ch: Joe Liggins and back to Kid Ory
641.q: That's right. It wasn't Natchez. You'd mention that to Bud Scott, and Bud would say, 'No, man, I ain't from Natchez. That fella in Natchez can't play nothin.' 'I'm the original,' he used to tell you. 'I'm from New Orleans.'

29.t: Jack McVea and his father Isaac McVea, guitarist and teacher
29.s: Howard describes Isaac McVea as a strong guitarist and teacher who led a party band with young players, including his son Jack.
29.ch: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
29.q: No personality, you might say. You didn't have to worry with him, because he'd tell you what he wanted and then he'd get it out of you. Did you hear that? He'd get it out of you, if you had it in you.

29.t: 1974: Mr. McVea's band and the priests who threw dollars
29.s: Howard describes Isaac McVea as a banjo player, a fine man to work for, though priests once threw dollars at his head.
29.q: (Unintelligible) But I mean when you let things like that go it's not too good, you know. But other than that Mr. McVea was a pretty nice man. And he had -- he had -- well, he didn't have no style of playing or anything like that.

384.s: He describes guitarist Eddie Lang as someone who kept everything in his head and did not need to read, close to Joe Venuti.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: He could but he didn't have to. So the people that we played for always wrote out the thing that we were supposed to play.

384.t: The Chicago Loopers record and guitarist Carl Kress
384.s: Kline lists the Chicago Loopers session with Bix; Morehouse and Virginia praise Carl Kress as a guitarist as good as Eddie Lang.
384.ch: Bix, Trumbauer and the Goldkette sidemen
384.q: Very close friend. Chauncey admired Carl Kress. He felt he was the finest guitarist there was.

169.s: McGhee describes Christian's natural feeling and tune 'Solo Flight', and meeting him in 1933-34.
169.ch: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
169.q: Well, I'll tell you what. Charlie Christian helped a lot. He helped Oklahoma quite a bit as far as the sound is concerned. Because he had a thing going which was natural for him, but I mean, like that was really a natural for everybody that listened to what he was playing. Like, when he came out of…

169.t: Christian's unamplified playing, Goodman and Minton's
169.s: He played an acoustic guitar then; Minton's kept an amp for him.
169.ch: Writing, Oklahoma roots and the origins of bebop
169.q: Well, he was something, boy. I really loved him. When I heard him, I couldn't hardly believe that a man could sound that good, you know. But he was really taking care of business when I met him.

455.t: Southern Serenaders in Oklahoma City: Hot Lips Page, Rushing and Walter Page
455.s: The band that rescues the boys includes Hot Lips Page, Bill Owens, Walter Page, Jimmy Rushing, and young Charlie Christian.
455.q: for him. We didn't last too long, but in order to get back we went into Oklahoma City and we met, at that time, this same band that I was talking about, the Southern Serenaders.

455.t: When Budd first met Charlie Christian
455.s: Hinton and Budd sort out the date of Budd's first meeting with Charlie Christian, before John Hammond discovered him.
455.q: Oh, I don't know. I -- you see, because in the 30's I left Dallas for good in '28, which I was -- I'm going to come to. But then I had met Charlie Christian, he was just a youngster, and --

171.t: Walter Page, Basie and Freddie Green: keeping out of each other's way
171.s: Page's balance ideas, one piano in Moten's band, Freddie Green's single chords and why bop dropped the guitar.
171.ch: Bass, drums and the big-band rhythm section
171.q: Uh-huh. Yeah. Now if you'll notice in Basie's band, that famous guitarist, Freddie Green, does not flirt with the chords, if you understand what I mean. You know, chords can and follow progressions. Chords can stay just on the rudiments, and that way people know where you are, and they don't have…

171.t: How the McShann rhythm section found each other; the guitar player
171.s: Influenced by Basie and above all Page, Ramey, McShann and Gus Johnson let the rhythm section walk alone; a guitarist was added in 1941.
171.ch: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
171.q: But we used to have our conferences and talk, and I would express to them what Page had told me, about how we could should team, how that bass drum drummer's foot shouldn't be too heavy, and how the bass player should stay away from trying to run every chord that goes along, but get a straight line…

239.t: Wes Montgomery: first hearing and the Kenton Neophonic score
239.s: Jones was stunned by Wes Montgomery's chordal playing and wrote a Neophonic work for him, mailing a guitar demo.
239.ch: Stuff Smith stories, Wes Montgomery and singers
239.q: first time I heard Wes play I didn't know whether to run or what, stand up and run. I'd never heard anybody play a guitar like that, you know? And --

239.t: The string album with Wes Montgomery and Kenny Burrell
239.s: A string date with two guitars, Hank Jones and Milt Hinton; Wes turned his music upside down and the strings tapped bows for him.
239.ch: Stuff Smith stories, Wes Montgomery and singers
239.q: Oh, boy, let me see. We did a string album, and I said, well, the people that I want -- I wanted two guitarists so I got Kenny Burrell.

173.t: Playing with Johnny Schenk's string band
173.s: Members of the Schenk string band (Deveread on bass, Williamson on guitar) and praise for Deveread's steady time. Albert Six and his Italian dialect recitation.
173.q: With Johnny Schenk. Well, Johnny Schenk. Well, nine times out of ten, the fellow John Deveread, uh, John Deveread, he used to play bass with him. And Johnny Williamson, he used to play guitar with him. Uh-huh. And he used to play violin. And then I'd play corners with him, you see? Uh-huh. But, uh,…

241.s: Answering Dick's questions, Valentine says banjoist Elton Theodore is older than he is, about 63-65, and has moved from his old address.
241.q: Well, I got his address at home. I got the address at home. I think I got that address at home. See, when we had this band here, we were living on Wyatt Street, you see? But now he don't live there no more now. He moved from there, you see? Oh yeah. Uh huh, yeah, he moved from there. I always can…

920.t: Banjos and guitars; Shields's St. Louis Blues chorus
920.s: Banjos came later with Whiteman, then Edwards reads an interpretation of Shields's chorus as his dislike of New York.
920.q: that weren't standing no not until uh Whiteman then came to banjo they had banjos of course but uh they didn't seem to not not not with a smaller band they were more like a solo instrument I often think of that chorus that uh Shields made on St. Louis Blues he was no doubt prompted by disdain and…

891.t: Guitar and banjo players: Jim Lucas, Walter, Freddie Gould
891.s: He discusses fingerpicking style, banjo player Jim Lucas who played with Rene, the blues picker Walter, and the crippled guitarist Freddie Gould.
891.q: Well in that time, them fellows would use just their fingers. I see here lately now, I see them fellows with them picks, you know, them sideline picks, but them fellows way back then, I mean they'd just be picking that with their fingers. I mean they'd play it too. Old fellow Jim Lucas, he used to…

178.t: Who led the band at the Tenors; guitarist Willie O'Connor
178.s: They try to recall bandleaders at the Tenors and a fine banjo and guitar player who taught others.
178.ch: Happy Land, sidemen and other bands
178.q: Let's see, who had that band that worked at the tenors? No, it was the Louis Daniels. No, wait, what year you was playing at? Oh, I don't know yet. I'll be frank, that's one thing I don't know yet.

172.t: George Sayles and six-string banjo players
172.s: Allen and Ridgley discuss George Sayles on guitar and viola, and six-string banjoists such as Johnny St. Cyr, Louis Keppard and John Marrero.
172.q: Yeah. He was a, him and I was back east. I was a violin player. And him and George Orton, I played together. Viola and violin.

861.t: Banjo, George Lewis and guitar players he admired
861.s: Johnson sat in on tenor banjo with George Lewis, credits Gassun Joseph, and praises Walter Nelson and Johnny St. Cyr on guitar.
861.q: I played tenor banjo with George Lewis' band when Morello was sick. Oh yeah. I played a lot of jobs, George, played ghetto, lack of benefit since rock.

182.t: Guitar picking technique and first tunes
182.s: Tom explains he picked with all his fingers and the thumb, played little tunes, and made his own band once he took up violin.
182.q: With my fingers, yeah. When you're playing in the band you have a little piece of, you know, you should sing, but I know the band. I only just pick, it was a pick of guitar.

255.t: Cousin Joseph, a guitarist who knows Buddy Bolden lore
255.s: He suggests interviewing his wife's cousin Joseph, an elderly family guitarist who knows old songs and Buddy Bolden stories.
255.ch: First jobs and New Orleans players
255.q: Well, nobody. All of them played string instruments. I got a cousin now. He play guitar now. He's about 78 or 80 years old. He learned how my father's guitar. One of my first cousins. He's still playing. Yeah. He's in town? He's in town now.

772.t: Favorite banjo players in New Orleans
772.s: Asked about banjo players he admired, Hamilton names a Marrero and the fast Poise Sevier; he never took up guitar.
772.q: Well it was a fella, there were two fellas that I know, one of them was one of those Marrero, but it wasn't Lawrence.

773.t: Bands she heard before marriage; Charlie Bocage and his banjo song
773.s: She recalls a band from over the river and Charlie Bocage, who played little banjo and sang a song about shoes.
773.ch: Early music and the Olympia band
773.q: Did you listen to music? Oh, yeah, there was... Some band came from over the river, but I can't place them. And they was a fine band, too. They was from over the river. They was with, uh, how do you call that fellow? Oh, Charlie Bokauer, the Bokauer's. Oh, I know them. Yeah, I heard them, you know.…

662.t: Celestin's hiring and the banjo-piano pairing
662.s: Celestin hired replacements himself, favoring readers. He usually kept both banjo and piano; her husband later became the regular banjoist.
662.q: Well, he would hire the replacements whenever there was an opening. I mean if anybody had to lay off or something like that he would hire a replacement but it would be someone who could read and use it.

969.s: Blanchin recalls Quinn later visiting the Grunewald music company and playing impressively.
969.q: Well, truthfully, my interest wasn't great enough at that time to actually say that he was a great musician then. Of course, I know later that he did become a very great musician. But at that time, I wouldn't have been qualified to judge him anyway, I don't suppose.

265.t: Guitar players and serenaders: Rabbit, Walter, Noon and Sam
265.s: He knows Rabbit, Walter and Noon, who serenaded; serenading has dropped off and he has not seen Sam.
265.q: Well I know all them fellas, Rabbit and this boy Walter down there, he'd run that place down there, I'm telling you not. He's a bartender there now. Now I don't know if Noon stopped playing, is he playing yet? Yeah he's playing. He's playing yet? He plays yet? Huh? But no, there was a kick, so them…

266.t: Banjoists Amy Sharp and Buzzy, and the Mummers-style banjo bands
266.s: Jones praises Amy Sharp's rhythm banjo and Buzzy's technique, and they discuss how the old mummers banjo bands turned from playing tunes to sing-along schtick.
266.q: Yeah. You use her how often now? Right now she's working three days a week. While Buzzy was out during the summer with the center stage or whatever it is. She was working six days a week for about two months.

267.t: Guitar Slim's capo and tuning, and John Lee Hooker
267.s: On the new reel Ford explains how Slim used a capo-like key selector rather than retuning, and mentions playing with John Lee Hooker.
267.ch: On the road with Guitar Slim
267.q: Well, now, guitar slim, I'll take it from him. He played what you call a choke guitar. He had a selector, a key selector. He played in actually one key. But he had a key selector. I see a lot of these rock players now. You slide it up and down. A capo, it's called a capo, but we call it a choke.…

269.t: Spanish and Cuban people and guitar music
269.s: She says there were many Cubans and Spanish families and plenty of guitar.
269.q: Plenty, they had plenty, Cubans most so. And they had several Spanish families that I knew of. Then after that, those that came would not read Spanish, they were Cubans.

2.t: Guitar versus banjo and the sound of Preservation Hall guitarists
2.s: Allen and Russell on Sales's guitar, Bud Scott and Ory's band using guitar, and the dynamics of old bands.
2.q: Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of…

817.t: Preferred rhythm section and early piano-less groups
817.s: He likes banjo for its clean beat, and says early groups used banjo or guitar because pianos were scarce.
817.q: Like a banjo. Of course, I get along well with the guitar players, but I like to hear a banjo. I like that nice, clean beat that it provides and the way it cuts through the rhythm section. You know, it can be heard well and it's very pronounced.

970.t: February 1935 photo on Dumaine Street; rehearsals and Ernest Pinn
970.s: A February 1935 photo of the band was taken on Dumaine Street near the boxing arena where they rehearsed; Paul praises banjoist Ernest Pinn, who lost his mind and died.

614.ch: The Second Herd and its sidemen
614.q: Oh, yeah, very. And the only time he gave out was in his music. But everything else, he was very in himself and he had complexes and things. For awhile, while we were (inaudible) touring theatres, he said there was a guy following the band around, kept sitting in the balcony.

87.t: Eddie Durham finds Charlie Christian in Oklahoma City
87.s: With Lunceford, the band heard a guitarist in a club; Eddie Durham went to cut him and found Charlie Christian.
87.ch: Learning the trombone and jam sessions
87.q: Anywhere. On the road. I remember one day we were in Oklahoma City, and we were playing Oklahoma City. So, we were in a little club. I was with Lunceford and we heard this guitar player. Man, he was playing so much. So, Eddie Durham was with Lunceford's band.

677.s: Brown remembers Django's three-fingered playing and his guest spots in France and the United States.
677.ch: Ellington colleagues, singers and world tours
677.q: we ran into a real terrific guitar player. Django didn't have but three fingers. Yeah, he had three fingers and he would impossible things with those three fingers on guitar. But he was from -- he was a gypsy, really. So he didn't stay over here very long, just made a tour or two but he stayed…

17.t: Dick McDonough, Carl Kress and other studio players
17.ch: Rhythm Club memories and playing technique
17.q: Studio players and then outside jazz players. Yeah they were excellent musicians. But they could also get down and play ad lib some good jazz, especially Carl Kress, McDonough too, both of them were very good, well rounded musicians.

27.t: Paul Jones plays I Got Rhythm; Chester Brown's acoustic guitar
27.s: Paul Jones took seven or eight choruses on I Got Rhythm over an hour and a half and Chester Brown soloed single-note on acoustic guitar in a Charlie Christian style.
27.q: : First they was playing "I Got Rhythm." They played that about an hour-and-a-half -- heh-heh! He used to take about 7 or 8 choruses on it.

146.s: Asked about guitarist Efferge Ware, Smith names Christmas, Claude Williams, Jim Daddy Walker and Cliff.
146.q: No, there wasn't but two guitar players that I knew... No, wait a minute. There's three. There was one called Christmas. He's still living, he's still there. Then Fiddler -- Claude Williams. He's still there. We just played together last year. And there's a boy there called there Jim Daddy, a big…

166.t: Booker T. Pittman, the Pettifords and guitar battles in Oklahoma City
166.s: Recalls Oklahoma musicians and the battles between Jim Dandy and Charlie Christian.
166.ch: Family background and the Tulsa music scene
166.q: Well, I remember a distant relative of Booker T. Washington. His name was Booker T. Pittman. He played alto saxophone. He had a sort of a Indian complexion, hair that went along with it. And when I got to New York, he was just retiring. I got to hear him at Cafe Society, just as I got to New York,…

90.t: T-Bone Walker at the Three Sixes
90.s: First seeing T-Bone Walker at the Three Sixes and crediting him with opening up guitar playing.

381.t: Meeting Cozy Cole, Les Paul and Charlie Christian
381.s: On his third night he heard Cozy Cole at a club on 142nd Street and played behind Les Paul and Charlie Christian.
381.q: And then, like the third night, that was the first time I ran in to Cozy Cole. There was a club at 142nd Street, and 7th Avenue -- oh my God, I can't remember, right down the street from the Woodside Hotel. The guy that had the group, and it was Freddie Moore; Freddie Moore, the drummer. Freddie…

147.t: Jelly Roll Morton, riverboat bands and Alphonso Trent's sidemen
147.s: Crawford never met Jelly Roll Morton, recalls the levee bands, and describes Alphonso Trent's sidemen such as banjoist Crooke.
147.q: Oh. No, I didn't, but I knew a lot about him. I didn't have the pleasure of meeting him. But as I said, coming up in those river boat bands, they were natural musicians, sound, color, they were just -- it was amazing to stand on that levee in Memphis, Tennessee and listen to those bands coming…

453.t: Why banjo and tuba came back in the 1933 band
453.s: Asked why the rhythm section returned to banjo and tuba, Randolph thinks it was McKendrick's idea.
453.q: Well, let's see, Bill Oldham did have a tuba, I believe. But he didn't have it in the '34 band. See, I had the Oldham boys in that last band, too.

233.t: Seeing Wes at the Jazz Workshop
233.s: After a Tjader concert Monk squeezed into the Workshop and saw Wes was clearly on his way.
233.q: : When Wes came out and made a...and I could really see the impact of what was happening. And it was so strong, it was so definite. There was no question about it, he was on his way. They worked at Jazz Workshop. The night he worked at Jazz Workshop, I was playing a concert with Cal over at --…

99.t: Outcome of the battle, Floyd Smith's blues and the band's theme song
99.s: Floyd Smith's blues guitar and the popular theme song win the crowd; Pillars wires booking agents including Joe Glaser but nothing happens.
99.q: that now. They respected us from that time on. When they got back up on the bandstand, they were just lost, because -- in fact, everybody in our band had big tones, you know. And they blew those tones out. And we had this little Floyd Smith, and he could play that guitar. And he would play the…

454.t: Electric guitar, Larry Coryell and John Scofield
454.s: Mingus softens on electric instruments and likes Coryell and Scofield from Three or Four Shades of Blues.
454.ch: Sidemen, the Hampton years, race and money
454.q: Yeah, he plays. I was in Switzerland when I heard him on television with that guitar player, the other guitar player that was on a date with him. (Philip Catherine-ed.)

168.t: Playing with Charlie Christian at Timme Rosenkrantz's apartment
168.s: Stewart played a couple of sessions with Charlie Christian at Rosenkrantz's 52nd Street pad and found him down to earth and a beautiful player.
168.q: -- he used to give little sessions at his pad on 52nd Street, he used to live, and a lot of the cats I met through these sessions, you know. So that's where --

388.t: Joining Eddie Condon's band and its rhythm section
388.s: Condon hires Leeman, letting him send subs on Saturdays; he praises Gene Schroeder, Bob Casey and Walter Page, whom he recommended, and Condon's unamplified guitar.
388.q: But I was approached by Eddie Condon who said why aren't you at Nick's, and I said they wouldn't let me off on Saturday night for a couple hours so I could do my Hit Parade, which I was just starting to do. Record dates in New York, and everybody was recognizing me, because I'm on the Hit Parade.

74.t: Eugene Crooke's banjo and how Driggs met him
74.s: Praise for Crooke's harp-like banjo sound; Driggs met him through Buddy Tate.
74.ch: Trent's band: Arkansas, Dallas and the Adolphus
74.q: We had a thing going doing that. Crook would make his banjo sound like a harp. He had something that nobody else had on that thing. It's hard to explain.

75.t: Why New York bands needed arrangements; drums and guitar
75.s: Harlem audiences wanted variety beyond the Blues, with West Indians, Puerto Ricans and Cubans in the mix; trap drummer and guitar traditions.
75.q: Yeah. And we also are speaking about bands that, when they came to New York, their music changed, and they had to get arrangements with much more variations than the Blues, you know -- more kind of things. Here you had bands like Don Redman, Benny Carter, Teddy Hill, Fletcher Henderson, and these…
